paras: The expulsion of Black residents from Jeanerette, Louisiana, took place in late August 1903, when white residents of the Iberia Parish town ordered dozens of Black people to leave after a Black barber, Louis Nicks, was accused of fatally shooting a white merchant, Joseph Sanders. Most of those ordered out left at once and were warned never to return, while a crowd searched the town's Black section and wire reports said Nicks would be lynched if caught. Deputies instead arrested Nicks at Baldwin on August 26, and he was lodged in the parish prison at New Iberia with no reported attempt on his life.

Joseph Amede Sanders kept a store in Jeanerette, and Louis Nicks, also spelled Nix and known as "Tilou," was a barber who lived near the Southern Pacific depot. About eight o'clock on the night of Sunday, August 23, Sanders was shot, and he died at his residence at 12:30 the next day.

Sheriff George Henderson of Iberia Parish and his deputies pursued Nicks from early on August 24, and several men arrested during the search proved to be the wrong party. A Franklin dispatch of August 25 said Nicks had left the train at Baldwin for the Cypremont Swamp, where his relatives lived, armed with the pistol used in the shooting.

Meanwhile about twenty-five or thirty Black residents were notified to leave Jeanerette, and a local dispatch said most "did not wait for a second invitation" and were warned never to return. A wire report put the number at "several score," ordered out "by the white people," while a New Orleans dispatch to the New York Sun said thirty people regarded as "worthless" were ordered out by "a committee of citizens." On the night of August 24 the Black section of town was "thoroughly searched"; the same dispatch reported angry mutterings but called the crowd "orderly and quiet." Reports from Jeanerette said race feeling was running high, that "it would take very little to precipitate a bloody riot," and that if caught Nicks would "never see the inside of a jail."

Deputy Sheriffs Alfred Pecot and Dudley Sanders arrested Nicks at Baldwin on the morning of Wednesday, August 26, and Sheriff Henderson brought him to New Iberia on the afternoon train. A large crowd gathered at the jail yard after he arrived, but the New Iberia Enterprise reported "no demonstration of unusual nature" and predicted a "speedy trial and punishment." The Weekly Iberian last described Nicks as held "awaiting trial"; no report of a trial or sentence appears in the coverage.

The episode was carried by white Louisiana weeklies and by short wire items in papers elsewhere, and no account in the Black press appears in the coverage. The first wire story, printed in the Paducah Sun on August 25 under the headline "Killed by a Tough," called Nicks "a negro tough" and stated flatly that "a lynching will follow his capture." A second wire item ran as "Negroes Ordered Out" in the Opelousas St. Landry Clarion and "Negroes Ordered to Leave" in the Pine Bluff Daily Graphic. The New York Sun titled its dispatch "Thirty Worthless Negroes Banished," taking up the expellers' description of those driven out, and the Winnfield Southern Sentinel headed its brief "Shot By a Black-Buck."

The New Iberia papers reprinted Jeanerette correspondence credited to "T. D." and to the Picayune of New Orleans, and only the local papers gave the versions in which Sanders struck first or Nicks was dazed in a general fight. That correspondence blamed "the worthless class of negroes who have of late years infested this section" and expected "summary punishment" for Nicks if caught.

Accounts of the shooting differed: the wire report said Nicks was fighting another Black man in Sanders's store and shot Sanders when he tried to stop the row. The Jeanerette correspondent quoted in the Weekly Iberian cited "reliable information" that the two men had quarreled and that Sanders struck Nix with a stick before Nix drew a revolver and shot him twice. After his arrest Nicks admitted the killing but, according to the St. Mary Banner, said it happened in a general fight in which he was knocked on the head and dazed.

reader.title: Expulsion of Black residents from Jeanerette, Louisiana
bases: After the shooting of a white merchant, white residents ordered between twenty-five and 'several score' Black residents to leave Jeanerette and warned them never to return, alongside a manhunt for the accused man with open talk of lynching (A7, A5, A2, A1).

A local Jeanerette dispatch (A7), a separate wire report (A5, A3) and a New Orleans dispatch (A2) agree that dozens of Black residents were ordered out after Sanders's killing; the shooting, pursuit and arrest are reported by several local papers (A6, A9, A10, A11).

framing.detail: Headed 'Killed by a Tough', called Nicks 'a negro tough' and said a lynching would follow his capture, without comment.
'Negroes Ordered Out' / 'Negroes Ordered to Leave': reports the expulsion and fear of a 'bloody riot' in wire language.
Headline 'Thirty Worthless Negroes Banished' adopts the expellers' description of those driven out; Nicks a 'negro desperado'.
Headline 'Shot By a Black-Buck'; Nicks a 'barber, gambler and tough'.
Local dispatches blame 'the worthless class of negroes who have of late years infested this section', stress that the searching crowd was orderly, and anticipate 'summary punishment'.
Reports the arrest, the crowd at the jail with no demonstration, and expects a 'speedy trial and punishment' of 'the wretch'.
Reports the arrest and gives Nicks's own account of a general fight.

versions.value: Nicks was fighting another Black man in Sanders's store and shot Sanders when he tried to stop the row
The two men quarreled, Sanders struck Nix with a stick, and Nix drew a revolver and shot him twice

conflicts.note: The stick version comes from the local correspondent citing 'reliable information'; Nix's version is his own and the wire's is unsourced. None is sworn testimony.
The local Jeanerette dispatch (A7) is the closest to the scene; 'several score' appears only in the wire copy.
Only the New Orleans dispatch names a committee; the local dispatch uses the passive 'have been notified'.
